#### Solution 1

Recall that a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$ has volume $V = \pi r^2 h$.

The original cylinder thus has volume $500\pi$, while the cylinders in choices (A), (B), (C), and (D) have volumes $2000\pi$, $1000\pi$, $250\pi$, and $4000\pi$ respectively.  So only the cylinder in choice $\boxed{\textbf{(B)}}$ has twice the volume of the original cylinder.

#### Solution 2

The volume of a cylinder is directly proportional to both its height and the square of its radius.

The cylinder in choice (A) has the same height as and twice the radius of the original, so its volume is $2^2 = 4$ times that of the original.

The cylinder in choice (B) has twice the height of and the same radius as the original, so its volume is $2$ times that of the original.

The cylinder in choice (C) has twice the height of and half the radius of the original, so its volume is $2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}$ of that of the original.

The cylinder in choice (D) has twice the height of and twice the radius of the original, so its volume is $2 \cdot 2^2 = 8$ times that of the original.

Therefore, only the cylinder in choice $\boxed{\textbf{(B)}}$ has twice the volume of the original cylinder.
